questions.stem: A 69-year-old man was admitted with MRSA pneumonia and bacteremia. He had a history of type 2 diabetes, controlled by diet alone. On admission his serum creatinine was 2.4 mg/dL and BUN 40 mg/dL. The patient’s most recent baseline serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen were 1.3 mg/dL and 25 mg/dL, respectively.
questions.lead_in: What antistaphylococcal agent would be most vulnerable to drug accumulation and associated increased risk of adverse effects in this patient?
questions.explanation: Telavancin The possible agents listed have variable coverage against MRSA, with linezolid and telavancin being most established for treatment of serious systemic MRSA infections. Clindamycin, minocycline, linezolid, and tigecycline do not require dosage adjustment in the setting of renal insufficiency. Therefore serum concentrations of these agents would not be expected to accumulate in this patient as a result of renal insufficiency. Telavancin is eliminated primarily by the kidneys and is also recognized as potentially nephrotoxic. This agent can accumulate in patients with renal insufficiency and increased risk of adverse effects.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q4

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman was diagnosed with methicillinresistant Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia and bacteremia approximately 48 hours after recovering from a case of uncomplicated influenza. She had a history of hyperlipidemia and depression. She had no known drug allergies. Medications prior to admission were atorvastatin 20 mg daily and citalopram 20 mg daily. Vancomycin 1250 mg IV q12 hours was initiated, with a serum trough concentration after the fourth dose of 16.1 μg/mL. While receiving the fifth dose of vancomycin, the patient experienced face and neck flushing and redness.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Decrease the vancomycin dose to 1250 mg q24 hours
Double the infusion time of subsequent vancomycin doses

questions.explanation: Double the infusion time of subsequent vancomycin doses Tigecycline achieves marginal serum concentrations and is not suitable for bloodstream infections. The current vancomycin dose of 1250 mg q12 hours provided a therapeutic trough concentration of 16.1 μg/mL and should not be reduced. Daptomycin is inactivated in pulmonary surfactant and is ineffective for pneumonia. Linezolid should be avoided in combination with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors due to risk of serotonin syndrome. This patient is likely experiencing red-man syndrome with vancomycin, which can typically be controlled by extending the length of each vancomycin infusion and/or premedicating with diphenhydramine.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q4

questions.stem: A 55-year-old patient was hospitalized in the surgical intensive care unit with septic shock following GI surgery. Comorbidities included atrial fibrillation, GERD, and hypertension. The patient had no known drug allergies. Medications included amiodarone, aspirin, cefepime, dabigatran, esomeprazole, heparin, vancomycin. The patient’s weight and height were 60 kg and 65 inches, respectively. Investigations: Fungal blood cultures grew Candida, speciation pending Creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (baseline SCr 1.1 mg/dL) ALT 15 units/L EKG: QTc 480 ms
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Micafungin Due to this patient being critically ill and the possibility of azole-resistant Candida, when Candida speciation and susceptibilities are unknown, empiric coverage with an echinocandin-like micafungin is recommended. Additionally, micafungin is not known to prolong the QTc interval. All of the azoles, except for isavuconazole, have a risk of prolonging the QTc interval. Terbinafine does not have a role in the treatment of disseminated candidiasis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q8

questions.question: Give one theoretical pharmacokinetic advantage of regimen A over regimen B.
questions.question_raw: 31. Give one theoretical advantage of regimen A over regimen B based on pharmacokinetics.

parts.text: Gram-negative acute pyelonephritis: A) gentamicin once daily vs B) gentamicin thrice daily
Pseudomonas pneumonia with elevated but still-susceptible MIC to piperacillin-tazobactam: A) piperacillin-tazobactam continuous infusion vs B) piperacillin-tazobactam in separate doses
MRSA bacteremia: A) vancomycin thrice daily vs B) vancomycin twice daily

parts_raw.text: For Gram negative acute pyelonephritis: A: Gentamicin once daily, B: Gentamicin thrice daily
b) For Pseudomonas pneumonia with increased MICs, but not resistant to PIP-TAZO: A: Pip-Tazo in a continuous infusion, B: Pip-Tazo in separate doses
c) For MRSA bacteremia: A: Vancomycin thrice daily, B: Vancomycin twice daily

questions.model_answer: a) Aminoglycoside killing is concentration-dependent: a single large daily dose maximizes peak/MIC (efficacy rises to ~90% at peak/MIC >8) and exploits the PAE, while saturable proximal-tubular uptake means once-daily dosing deposits less drug in the renal cortex, lowering/delaying nephrotoxicity. b) Piperacillin-tazobactam killing is time-dependent (T>MIC); continuous infusion keeps free drug above the (elevated) MIC for the whole interval, maximizing bacterial exposure. c) Vancomycin efficacy tracks 24-h AUC/MIC; more frequent (thrice-daily) dosing raises AUC/MIC to hit target for MRSA.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the aminoglycoside rationale is drawn from this chapter; the piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin points rest on standard beta-lactam/glycopeptide PK/PD.

cohort_answer.text: Once-daily gentamicin rationale: Aminoglycoside bactericidal activity is concentration dependent - higher peak/MIC ratio gives greater rate/extent of kill; goal is to maximize drug concentration at site of infection (optimum when exposure is ~8-10x MIC). Aminoglycosides exhibit a post-antibiotic effect (PAE, 0.5-8hrs). Saturable uptake in renal tubule cell/inner ear - once daily dosing gives lower renal cortical tissue concentration than divided/continuous dosing. Adaptive resistance (first exposure effect) - down-regulation of uptake after initial exposure; longer dosing interval preserves antibacterial activity. Decreases emergence of resistant subpopulations when peak is ≥8x MIC. Continuous Pip-Tazo infusion: maintains drug levels above MIC longer (time-dependent killing), better for bugs with minimal PAE. Vancomycin TID vs BID: killing depends on 24hr AUC/MIC; more frequent dosing gives higher AUC/MIC and better killing. NB. Vancomycin is cleared renally so actual dosing depends on weight/CrCl; goal trough >15 in severe infections.

questions.question: Telavancin: describe two mechanisms of action.

parts.text: Describe two mechanisms of action of telavancin.

parts_raw.text: Telavancin, describe two mechanisms of action.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Inhibition of cell wall (peptidoglycan) synthesis: like vancomycin, telavancin binds the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of lipid-II peptidoglycan precursors, blocking transglycosylation and transpeptidation. (2) Disruption of bacterial membrane integrity: the lipophilic decylaminoethyl side chain anchors in and causes concentration-dependent depolarization of the cytoplasmic membrane, increasing permeability with leakage of ATP and K+, contributing to rapid bactericidal killing.
questions.beyond_mandell: Telavancin mechanism-of-action is in the Mandell Ch. 30 lipoglycopeptide section, beyond the provided slice (pp. 377-388).

cohort_answer.text: Potent inhibitor of cell wall synthesis - inhibits d-ala-d-ala (more potent); Disrupts cell membrane integrity

questions.model_answer: a) Aminoglycosides kill in a concentration-dependent fashion: a single high daily dose maximizes peak/MIC (efficacy ~90% at peak/MIC >8, with less emergence of resistance) and exploits the PAE, while saturable proximal-tubular uptake lowers renal cortical accumulation and delays nephrotoxicity. b) Piperacillin-tazobactam is time-dependent (T>MIC); continuous infusion keeps free concentration above the elevated MIC throughout the interval, maximizing exposure. c) Vancomycin efficacy is driven by 24-h AUC/MIC; thrice-daily dosing raises AUC/MIC toward target for MRSA.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the gentamicin rationale is from this chapter; piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin points rest on standard beta-lactam/glycopeptide PK/PD.

cohort_answer.text: Once-daily gentamicin: Higher dose gives higher concentration and post-antibiotic effect, more efficient killing; gentamicin is concentration-dependent (Cmax/MIC); PAE up to 2-6 hours in vitro, longer with higher peak; Cmax/MIC >8 correlates with less emergence of resistance; possibly lower risk of oto/nephrotoxicity. PipTazo continuous infusion: Time-dependent killing agent, greater efficacy with T>MIC; continuous infusion maintains concentrations above MIC longest, option for Pseudomonas with higher MICs. Vancomycin TID vs BID: Better area under the curve; efficacy best predicted by AUC/MIC ratio (combination of T>MIC and Peak:MIC); AUC24/MIC targets can be met with shorter interval dosing or increased dose

questions.model_answer: a) AUC-guided monitoring (24-hour AUC/MIC) rather than trough-only monitoring, for serious MRSA infections. b) AUC/MIC ratio of 400-600 mg*h/L (assuming a broth-microdilution MIC of 1 mg/L). c) (1) Bayesian estimation using pharmacokinetic software (can use as few as one, ideally two, levels) and (2) first-order pharmacokinetic (analytic) equations using two steady-state levels. d) Two vancomycin serum concentrations: a post-distribution peak and a trough (a Bayesian approach can be applied with a single trough).

questions.question: For gram-positive pathogens, name the following regarding β-lactam resistance and alternatives.

parts.text: Two mechanisms of β-lactam resistance.
Two alternative agents and their mechanism of action.

parts_raw.text: 2 mechanism of beta lactam resistance
2 alternative agent and their mechanism of action

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Production of a β-lactamase (penicillinase) that hydrolyzes the β-lactam ring, e.g. staphylococcal class A penicillinase. (2) Production of a low-affinity PBP that circumvents drug binding, e.g. PBP2a in methicillin-resistant staphylococci or PBP5 in Enterococcus faecium.
b) (1) Vancomycin - binds the terminal D-alanyl-D-alanine of peptidoglycan precursors, sterically blocking transglycosylation/transpeptidation (cell-wall synthesis). (2) Daptomycin - inserts into and depolarizes the cytoplasmic membrane in a calcium-dependent manner, causing loss of membrane potential and cell death. (Linezolid, binding 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit to inhibit protein synthesis, is an acceptable alternative.)
questions.beyond_mandell: The chapter grounds the two resistance mechanisms (β-lactamase; low-affinity PBP2a/PBP5) and names vancomycin as an alternative, but the detailed mechanisms of action of vancomycin/daptomycin/linezolid are established pharmacology from other chapters.

questions.question: Telavancin: name two mechanisms of action.

parts.text: Name two mechanisms of action of telavancin.

parts_raw.text: Name two mechanisms of action.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Inhibition of cell wall synthesis: binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors, blocking transglycosylation/transpeptidation (glycopeptide mechanism). (2) Membrane depolarization/disruption: the lipophilic side chain concentrates in the cytoplasmic membrane, causing concentration-dependent depolarization, loss of membrane potential, and increased permeability with leakage of ATP and K+ - giving rapid bactericidal activity.
questions.beyond_mandell: Telavancin mechanism-of-action is in the Mandell Ch. 30 lipoglycopeptide section, beyond the provided slice (pp. 377-388).

cohort_answer.text: Lipoglycopeptide, semisynthetic derivative of glycopeptides with dual mechanism: 1) Binds to peptidoglycan precursor outside bacterial cell, inhibiting cell wall synthesis; 2) Rapid concentration-dependent depolarization of cell membrane causing ATP/potassium leakage and cell death. Eliminated by kidney, requires dose adjustment; adverse reactions: QT prolongation, nephrotoxicity, red man syndrome, rash, interferes with coagulation tests; potential teratogenic effect

questions.model_answer: a) Once-daily gentamicin: maximizes peak/MIC (concentration-dependent kill, less resistance at peak/MIC >8), exploits the PAE, and reduces renal cortical accumulation via saturable uptake, lowering/delaying nephrotoxicity; also simpler and cheaper. b) Thrice-daily gentamicin: needed for synergy dosing in enterococcal endocarditis, and allows peak/trough monitoring where PK is unpredictable (burns, pregnancy, altered volume of distribution). c) Continuous piperacillin-tazobactam: time-dependent killing, so extended infusion maximizes T>MIC, useful for organisms with elevated MICs. d) Intermittent (QID) piperacillin-tazobactam: convenience/practicality of administration. e) Thrice-daily vancomycin: raises 24-h AUC/MIC toward target for maximal killing. f) Twice-daily vancomycin: convenience, adherence, and potentially less toxicity.
questions.beyond_mandell: Aminoglycoside points are from this chapter; piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin points rest on standard PK/PD teaching.

cohort_answer.text: Once daily gentamicin: convenience/adherence, less renal toxicity risk (saturable proximal tubule accumulation), concentration-dependent killing, post-antibiotic effect. TID gentamicin: can monitor trough/peak levels for PK adjustment (burns, pregnancy, renal impairment), better for synergy in endocarditis. Pip-tazo continuous infusion: time-dependent killing supports extended-infusion dosing, increasing time over MIC. Pip-tazo QID: convenience of dosing. Vancomycin TID: killing depends on AUC/MIC, allows higher AUC/MIC for maximum bactericidal effect. Vancomycin BID: convenience, adherence, less toxicity risk

questions.question: Telavancin: two mechanisms of action.

parts.text: State two mechanisms of action of telavancin.

parts_raw.text: a) 2 mechanisms of action

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Inhibition of cell wall synthesis: a semisynthetic vancomycin derivative that binds peptidoglycan precursors at their D-Ala-D-Ala termini as they emerge from the cytoplasm, disrupting transglycosylation/transpeptidation and cross-linking. (2) Concentration-dependent depolarization of the bacterial cell membrane (via its lipophilic decylaminoethyl side chain), causing membrane disruption, ion (K+) leakage, disrupted ATP turnover, and increased permeability - key to its bactericidal activity.
questions.beyond_mandell: Telavancin mechanism-of-action is in the Mandell Ch. 30 lipoglycopeptide section, beyond the provided slice (pp. 377-388).

cohort_answer.text: Semisynthetic lipoglycopeptide derivative of vancomycin. 1) Binds peptidoglycan precursors (d-alanine-d-alanine termini) outside the bacterial cell as they emerge from the cytoplasm, disrupting peptidoglycan cross-linking and inhibiting cell wall synthesis (similar to vanco, but transglycosylase activity 10x that of vanco). 2) Rapid concentration-dependent depolarization of bacterial cell membrane - membrane disruption, leakage of ions (K+), disrupted ATP turnover, increased permeability, death; important for bactericidal activity.

questions.model_answer:
a) Compare banding patterns across the 9 lanes: isolates with identical band patterns are the same clone/strain, indicating a clonal outbreak with patient-to-patient (nosocomial) transmission; lanes differing by only a few bands are closely related subtypes, while those with many band differences are unrelated strains.
b) The contaminated hospital environment and equipment (bed rails, linen, doorknobs, bedpans, urinals, blood pressure cuffs, stethoscopes, monitoring equipment) and the hands, gloves, and gowns of health care workers, which are the most common source of transmission.
c) For VRE, acquisition of the vanA gene cluster, which produces peptidoglycan precursors terminating in D-alanine-D-lactate, markedly reducing vancomycin binding.
questions.beyond_mandell: The Tenover PFGE interpretation criteria are general molecular-epidemiology knowledge, not stated in this chapter.

questions.question: Staphylococcus aureus vancomycin resistance.

parts.text: Explain the mechanism of VISA and VRSA.
Give the MIC cut-offs.

parts_raw.text: Explain mechanism of VISA and VRSA.
Give MIC cut offs.

questions.model_answer: a) VISA: a chromosomally-mediated, stepwise adaptation - a markedly thickened, poorly cross-linked cell wall with an excess of free D-Ala-D-Ala termini and reduced autolytic activity; these decoy targets bind and sequester ("clog") vancomycin in the outer wall layers so it cannot reach the septal target. VRSA: acquisition of the vanA operon (transposon Tn1546) from vancomycin-resistant enterococci, which remodels the peptidoglycan terminus from D-Ala-D-Ala to D-Ala-D-Lac, abolishing vancomycin binding. b) VSSA MIC <=2 ug/mL; VISA MIC 4-8 ug/mL; VRSA MIC >=16 ug/mL (hVISA <=2 by routine MIC but harbours resistant subpopulations).
questions.beyond_mandell: CLSI vancomycin breakpoints and the detailed VISA/VRSA mechanism are in the Mandell resistance section that falls outside the provided page slice.

Gentamicin IV/IM 3 mg/kg/d in 2-3 divided doses, 2 weeks. Gentamicin should be administered for the initial 2 weeks of therapy with either beta-lactam or vancomycin-containing regimens; if a strain is resistant to gentamicin, a fluoroquinolone may be used if the strain is susceptible.

questions.question_raw: What is the mechanism of resistance for the following:

parts.text: Vancomycin-intermediate Staphylococcus aureus (VISA)
Fluoroquinolones in Streptococcus pneumoniae
Penicillin in Enterococcus faecium
Group A Streptococcus and erythromycin

parts_raw.text: VISA
FQ in Strep. pneumoniae
Penicillin in E. faecium
GAS & erythro

questions.model_answer: a) VISA: cell-wall changes (no enterococcal van genes) - a thickened cell wall whose excess D-Ala-D-Ala termini trap vancomycin in the outer peptidoglycan layers ('decoy'/clogging), plus increased cell-wall turnover, decreased autolytic activity, increased positive cell-wall charge, and reduced Agr function (mediated by mutations in TCSs such as GraSR, VraSR, WalKR). b) Fluoroquinolones in S. pneumoniae: stepwise target mutations in DNA gyrase (gyrA) and topoisomerase IV (parC/parE), plus efflux (PmrA). c) Penicillin/ampicillin in E. faecium: low-affinity penicillin-binding protein PBP5 - overexpression and/or mutation reducing beta-lactam binding. d) GAS + erythromycin: (1) erm-mediated ribosomal target methylation (23S rRNA) giving the MLSB phenotype and (2) mef-mediated macrolide efflux pump.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the VISA mechanism is in the slice (pp. 378-379); the S. pneumoniae fluoroquinolone, E. faecium PBP5, and GAS erm/mef mechanisms are from established Mandell/antimicrobial resistance knowledge (other chapters).

cohort_answer.text: VISA: Increased cell wall turnover. Increased thickness of cell wall and cross linking of peptidoglycan. S. pneumo with moxifloxacin - DNA gyrase, Topoisomerase IV. GAS with erythromycin - Erm gene - methylation of target site (MLSB phenotype); mef gene - efflux pump. E. faecium w/ penicillin: altered PBP5 - Overexpression

What are 2 first line therapy for MRSA, describe their mechanism of action

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Beta-lactamase (penicillinase) production - enzymatic hydrolysis of the beta-lactam ring. (2) Altered penicillin-binding protein/target-site modification - e.g. mecA-encoded PBP2a with low beta-lactam affinity (the MRSA mechanism). b) (1) Vancomycin - a glycopeptide that binds the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala of peptidoglycan precursors, blocking transglycosylation and transpeptidation and thereby cell-wall synthesis. (2) Daptomycin - a cyclic lipopeptide that inserts (calcium-dependently) into the bacterial cell membrane, causing depolarization and loss of membrane potential with ion (K+) efflux and rapid cell death.

cohort_answer.text: Mechanisms of resistance: Beta lactamase production; PBP mutations - target site modification. MRSA first line therapy: Vancomycin - glycopeptide that caps the dAla-dAla terminus of the PG chain preventing transpeptidation; Daptomycin - lipoglycopeptide that inserts into the bacterial cell membrane leading to depolarization followed by ion leakage

What is the MIC for VISA?
Describe the mechanism of resistance of VISA as it applies to (1) the cell wall and (2) vancomycin.

parts_raw.text: How would you define heterogeneous vancomycin-intermediate Staphylococcus aureus?
What is the MIC for VISA?
describe the mechanism of resistance of VISA as it applies to 1) the cell wall 2) Vancomycin?

questions.model_answer: a) hVISA: an isolate that tests vancomycin-susceptible by routine MIC methods (MIC <=2 ug/mL) but that contains minority subpopulations of cells able to grow at intermediate concentrations (4-8 ug/mL); detected by population analysis profile (PAP-AUC), it is regarded as the precursor phenotype to VISA. b) VISA MIC 4-8 ug/mL. c) (1) Cell wall: markedly thickened, poorly cross-linked peptidoglycan with an excess of free (unlinked) D-Ala-D-Ala termini and reduced autolytic activity. (2) Vancomycin: those surplus D-Ala-D-Ala decoy targets bind and trap ("clog") vancomycin in the thick outer wall, sequestering the drug so it cannot diffuse to the active site of cell-wall synthesis at the septum/membrane - i.e. affinity trapping rather than target substitution.
questions.beyond_mandell: hVISA definition, MIC breakpoints and VISA mechanism are in the Mandell resistance section that falls outside the provided page slice.

questions.model_answer: a) Hospital A: 2000 g / 2 g = 1000 DDD; (1000 / 4000) x 1000 = 250 DDD per 1000 patient-days. b) Hospital B: (2000 days of vancomycin / 2000 patient-days) x 1000 = 1000 DOT per 1000 patient-days. c) Cannot be determined from these numbers alone — DDD-based use is identical (both 250 DDD/1000 patient-days), and valid comparison requires similar patient populations, case-mix, and formulary. d) (1) Patients requiring dose adjustment (e.g., renal impairment), where DDD misrepresents exposure. (2) Pediatric patients (weight-based dosing not reflected by the adult DDD).

questions.question: Vancomycin-intermediate and vancomycin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

parts.text: State the VISA vancomycin MIC and the reason for resistance.
State the VRSA vancomycin MIC and the reason for resistance.

parts_raw.text: VISA MIC and reason for resistance
VRSA MIC and reason for resistance

questions.model_answer:
a) VISA: vancomycin MIC 4-8 mg/L. Mechanism is a thickened cell wall with excess unlinked D-ala-D-ala peptidoglycan termini that act as decoy binding sites, trapping vancomycin in the outer wall and preventing it from reaching its target ("clogging"), allowing ongoing cross-linking.
b) VRSA: vancomycin MIC >=16 mg/L. Mechanism is acquisition of the vanA operon on transposon Tn1546 from vancomycin-resistant enterococci, which replaces the terminal D-ala-D-ala with D-ala-D-lactate, markedly reducing vancomycin binding affinity.
questions.beyond_mandell: VISA/VRSA MIC breakpoints (CLSI) and the thickened-wall vs vanA/Tn1546 mechanisms are from the glycopeptide-resistance section outside this page slice.

cohort_answer.text: VISA MIC 4-8 - altered thickening of cell wall with false binding sites, preventing vancomycin from reaching target sites and allowing ongoing cross linkage to occur in cell wall. VRSA MIC 16 - acquired transposon Tn1546 from VRE, causing synthesis of an alternative cell wall terminal peptide (D-ala-D-lac) rather than the normal terminal peptide (D-ala-D-ala), making vanco unable to bind to the cell wall
